title: The Savings Bond Gift Has Three Roles: Purchaser, Owner, Beneficiary
subtitle: For U.S. Series EE and I bonds, the person who pays, the person who owns the bond and the person named to receive it later may not be the same. That distinction can shape control and federal tax reporting.
imageAlt: Three generations of a family sit around a table, looking together at a savings bond record and writing down who purchased it, who owns it and who is named as beneficiary.
imageConcept: A close, natural-light view of three adult family members across generations at a kitchen table, with a laptop displaying a generic Treasury account screen, a handwritten three-column note labeled purchaser, owner and beneficiary, and a pen being passed between them. body: A gift can have three different names

A savings bond given within a family can feel straightforward: one person pays, another receives it, and the gesture is understood. But the bond’s registration—the ownership information attached to it—can separate those roles. The purchaser is the person who paid. The owner is the person registered as owning and controlling the bond. A beneficiary is named to receive it after the owner dies. These may be three different people, or some roles may overlap.

That distinction matters for U.S. Series EE and I savings bonds because registration is not just a label for the family’s records. It helps determine who has authority over the bond and can affect who reports its interest for federal income-tax purposes. A parent can buy a bond registered only to a child, for example, while being named as beneficiary. In that arrangement, paying for the bond does not by itself make the parent its owner. [1]

The practical starting point is to look at the registration rather than rely on family shorthand such as “the bond I gave them.”
The owner is not simply the person who paid

Imagine a grandparent buys a bond and registers a grandchild as its sole owner, with the grandparent listed as beneficiary. The grandparent funded the purchase and is named in the record, but the grandchild is the registered owner. The IRS says interest on a savings bond registered only in a child’s name is generally income to the child, even when a parent bought it and is named as beneficiary. [1]

This example is useful because it separates two ideas families often merge: contributing money and holding ownership rights. A beneficiary designation does not make the beneficiary a co-owner during the owner’s life. Nor does paying for a bond automatically put the purchaser in control of it. The details of registration matter, and the exact rights and procedures depend on the bond’s record and applicable Treasury rules.

For a family reviewing a bond, write down the names and roles as they appear in the Treasury record or on the bond. If the record is unclear, treat that as a question to resolve—not an invitation to assume that the person who paid has authority to change or cash it.
A beneficiary is a future handoff, not a second owner

Naming a beneficiary can help specify who is intended to receive the bond when its owner dies. But it does not give that person the same present role as an owner. That difference is especially important when a family is trying to make a gift available to a child while retaining the ability to manage it. A beneficiary designation is not a substitute for registering another person as an owner, and it should not be described as shared ownership.

The tax picture after an owner’s death also needs care. The treatment of savings-bond interest can depend on how the deceased owner reported income and on choices made by an executor, including whether accrued interest is reported on the final return. It is therefore too simple to say that every dollar of interest accumulated before death automatically becomes taxable income to the beneficiary. The IRS’s guidance for survivors and executors describes factors that affect the reporting. [3]

For families, the useful lesson is not to guess how a future transfer will be taxed. Keep the bond information with other financial records, and make sure the person who may handle the estate knows where to find it.
Changing registration can have tax consequences

A family may decide that an existing bond should be registered differently: perhaps a parent wants to remove their name, add or change a beneficiary, or move the bond into a trust. Those changes are not all equivalent. A beneficiary update is not necessarily the same as transferring ownership, and changing who is registered as owner can trigger consequences that the family did not anticipate.

Treasury’s reissue form for savings bonds warns that removing a living owner’s name can require that owner to report previously unreported interest for the year of reissue. [2] The form is a reminder to check the tax effect before treating a change as a clerical fix. 

Before submitting a reissue request, identify what the family is trying to accomplish, read the current Treasury form and instructions, and ask a qualified tax professional about the specific facts if the tax treatment is uncertain. Avoid signing or filing a change solely because it seems to make the account easier to manage.
Education rules make the registration question concrete

Families sometimes buy savings bonds with education costs in mind. Federal rules provide a possible interest exclusion for certain Series EE and I bonds used for qualified higher-education expenses, but it is conditional—not an automatic feature of naming a student as beneficiary. The qualifying bond generally must be registered in the taxpayer’s name, or, for a married taxpayer filing jointly, in the taxpayer’s and spouse’s names. The owner must also have been at least 24 before the bond was issued, along with other requirements. [1]

That means a bond registered in a child’s name does not qualify for this exclusion through a parent merely because the parent paid for it or plans to use the money for tuition. The registration and the other eligibility rules need to line up with the tax filer claiming the exclusion.

This is a good reason to think through the purpose of a bond before choosing its registration. It is not a reason to assume that one setup is best for every family: control, intended recipient, timing and tax circumstances all matter. A tax professional can help assess eligibility using current rules and the household’s circumstances.
A short review before the bond changes hands

A calm, practical review can prevent confusion later. First, locate the bond’s current record through the appropriate Treasury channel. Then make a three-column note: who paid for it, who is registered as owner, and who is named as beneficiary. Record the bond type and any available issue or purchase information, but keep account numbers and other sensitive details somewhere secure.

Next, ask what the family wants the bond to do. Is the intention to give a child ownership now, to name someone to receive it after the owner’s death, or simply to save for a future expense? Those goals are different, and the registration may not match the family’s assumptions. If someone proposes changing the record, identify whether the change affects ownership, beneficiary status or both, and check the current Treasury instructions before acting.

Finally, note unresolved tax questions rather than trying to settle them from memory. This is a federal savings-bond and income-tax overview, not individualized tax, legal, estate or investment advice. State law may matter to estate questions, and complicated ownership or transfer decisions deserve qualified guidance.
Make the roles visible before making a change

At the next unhurried family check-in, put a blank sheet of paper on the table and make three headings: purchaser, owner, beneficiary. Choose one bond and fill in the names from its actual record—not from memory. Ask each person whether the written roles match what they thought the gift meant. If they do not, pause before changing anything. Write down the question in plain language, such as “Would removing this owner affect interest reporting?” or “Does this registration fit the education-tax rule we had in mind?” Then assign one person to check the current Treasury instructions and, if needed, ask a tax professional. Keep the finished note with the bond records, without putting sensitive account details on a sheet that everyone can see. The point is not to turn a family gift into paperwork; it is to make sure the gift’s meaning and its legal record are not quietly at odds.
